title: N3
notes: A converging thin lens brings parallel paraxial rays to a real focus; a diverging lens makes them spread as if from a virtual focus. The optical centre and principal foci lie on the principal axis.
With Cartesian convention and light travelling left to right, the thin-lens equation is 1/f=1/v−1/u. A real object has u<0; a real image has v>0.
Worked example: f=+15 cm and u=−30 cm give 1/v=1/15−1/30=1/30, so v=+30 cm. Magnification m=v/u=−1: real, inverted and same size.
A diverging lens has f<0 and forms a virtual, upright, diminished image of a real object. Ray diagrams check signs and whether an image can be caught on a screen.
Lens power is P=1/f when f is in metres. A short focal length means high magnitude of power, but image size still depends on object placement.
confusion: Do not use the mirror equation in a lens problem.
The simple lens equation assumes a thin lens and paraxial rays.

specificConditions: **Optical Principles:** The behavior of light is governed by the laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and refraction (Snell's law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂). These laws derive from Fermat's principle of least time.

**Wave Nature of Light:** Light exhibits wave phenomena including interference, diffraction, and polarization. These cannot be explained by ray optics alone and require wave optics. The wavelength λ and frequency f are related by c = λf.

**Approximations and Validity:** Ray optics (geometrical optics) is valid when object sizes ≫ wavelength λ. Wave optics is required when apertures or obstacles are comparable to λ. Quantum optics is needed for single-photon phenomena.
